Civil Law
SIV-il LAW
noun phrase
From Latin civilis (of citizens, of the state) + Old English lagu (law, ordinance). In Reformed theology, the civil law (or judicial law) denotes the third category of the Mosaic legislation—the specific case laws, penalties, and administrative statutes given by God to govern the theocratic polity of ancient Israel as a national community.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The civil law (also called the judicial or forensic law) is the third category of Mosaic legislation, distinct from the moral law (the Ten Commandments and their enduring moral principle) and the ceremonial law (Levitical sacrificial ordinances typologically pointing to Christ). The civil law constituted the specific national code of Israel as God’s covenant nation: case laws governing property (Exod. 21–22), judicial procedures (Deut. 16:18–20), penalties for crimes including capital offenses (Deut. 19:16–21), the administration of the Levitical tithe, the year of Jubilee, and the laws of warfare (Deut. 20). These statutes were given as “judgments” (mishpatim) for the governance of a particular nation covenanted to the LORD in a specific stage of redemptive history. The 1689 Baptist Confession (19.4) and the Westminster Confession (19.4) agree that the civil laws of Moses “expired together with the state of that people; not obliging any other now, further than the general equity thereof may require.” This means the specific penalties and administrative procedures of the Mosaic civil code are not directly binding on modern civil governments as law; however, the general equity—the underlying moral principles of justice that the civil laws embody—remains instructive for any government seeking to honor God’s justice. The civil law reflects what righteous justice looks like applied to social order, even as its exact terms expired with the theocracy.

Webster 1828 Definition

Civil law: the system of law adopted and used by a people or nation, as distinguished from natural law, criminal law, and ecclesiastical law; in theology, the judicial statutes given by God to govern the national polity of Israel.

expand to see more

CIV'IL LAW. (Theology) The judicial statutes enacted by God for the governance of the nation of Israel as a theocratic commonwealth; distinct from the moral law binding all nations and the ceremonial law fulfilled in Christ.

2. In Reformed theology, the third division of the Mosaic law—the case laws, penalty statutes, and administrative ordinances of the Sinaitic covenant polity, which expired with the dissolution of that national theocracy.

3. (General Equity) The principle that while the specific statutes of Israel's civil law have expired, the underlying principles of justice they embody are instructive for civil government under the light of natural law and general revelation.

4. Distinguished from natural law (written on the heart, binding all mankind) and from ecclesiastical law (governing the church by Christ's appointment).

Webster's theological framework, reflecting the Puritan tradition in which he was educated, assumed the tripartite division of Mosaic law as the foundation for civil jurisprudence.

Modern Corruption

Two opposite errors afflict the civil law: Reconstructionist theonomy attempts to reimpose Israel’s specific penal statutes on modern nations as binding law, while secular liberalism dismisses any theological grounding for civil law and regards biblical norms as purely private convictions with no public claim.

expand to see more

Christian Reconstructionism (Rushdoony, Bahnsen) holds that the Mosaic civil code—including its specific penalties for crimes like blasphemy, adultery, sabbath violation, and rebellious children—remains binding on all civil governments as the unchanging law of God. This position confuses the specific form of Mosaic civil statutes with the enduring general equity they embody. The 1689 and Westminster Confessions explicitly distinguish these: the form expired with the theocracy; the equity remains instructive. Theonomy also fails to reckon with the typological character of Israel’s theocracy as a type of the Kingdom of Christ—a type that finds its fulfillment not in modern nation-states but in the new covenant community.

Liberal secularism errs in the opposite direction, treating the moral content of civil law as purely the product of social contract, majoritarian preference, or pragmatic utility. This evacuates justice of its transcendent grounding and makes law a function of power rather than righteousness. The Reformed tradition, while not imposing the Mosaic judicial code as binding statute, insists that civil law is properly grounded in the natural moral law that all governments are accountable to honor—and that Scripture, especially the enduring moral principles of the Decalogue, provides the richest illumination of what natural law requires.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin civilis (of citizens) and Hebrew mishpatim (judgments, ordinances) together define the civil law as the ordering of a community’s common life under divine justice.

expand to see more

Latin civilis — of citizens, of the city; the root distinguishing the political/civil sphere from the ecclesiastical and domestic spheres

Hebrew mishpatim — judgments, case laws; the specific term for Israel's judicial statutes beginning in Exod. 21:1

Hebrew chuqqim — statutes, ordinances; the fixed regulations of the Mosaic code, many of which belong to the civil category

Latin iudicialis — judicial, pertaining to judgment; the alternative Reformation-era term for the civil law (Westminster Confession 19.4: “judicial laws”)

Latin aequitas — equity, fairness; the basis on which the Reformed tradition derives enduring guidance from Mosaic civil statutes even after their specific form has expired

Usage

"The civil law's expiration does not mean Israel's judicial code is irrelevant—its general equity illuminates principles of proportionate punishment, protection of the innocent, and the sanctity of life that every civil government under God is obligated to uphold."

"The tripartite division of Mosaic law (moral, ceremonial, civil) is a Reformed-confessional hermeneutical tool rooted in the distinction between laws that bind all men at all times, laws that pointed typologically to Christ, and laws that governed a specific national theocracy."

"Civil magistrates are bound by the natural moral law (accessible through conscience and confirmed in Scripture) but not by the specific statutes of Mosaic Israel—a principle that guards both against theocratic overreach and against the secular dissolution of justice's transcendent grounding."
